Instructions

• For related work and baselines:

  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.

Materials

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current recommender systems, particularly those relying on unique item identifiers (IDRec), face significant challenges regarding cold-start problems and poor knowledge transferability. While generative recommendation paradigms attempt to address this by leveraging Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs), they often struggle to bridge the gap between general linguistic knowledge and the specific needs of recommendation tasks. Furthermore, existing methods fail to effectively synthesize complementary knowledge from multimodal data (e.g., text and images). There is a lack of a unified representation framework that can seamlessly integrate heterogeneous modalities and domains to capture multi-faceted user preferences.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that transforming items from diverse domains and modalities into a single, unified "Quantitative Language" will serve as a universal bridge for recommendation knowledge transfer. By converting continuous, high-dimensional modality features into discrete, semantically meaningful tokens shared across a common vocabulary, we can treat recommendation as a sophisticated language generation task. We believe that training a model to "speak" this multimodal quantitative language will allow it to capture deeper semantic correlations between items and users, superior to methods that rely on arbitrary IDs or disjointed modal encoders.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a framework named **MQL4GRec** (Multimodal Quantitative Language for Generative Recommendation), which operates in three main phases:

**1. Quantitative Translators (The Vocabulary)**
We will design specific "translators" for each modality (text and image). Instead of using raw embeddings, we will employ a **Vector Quantization** approach (specifically a Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder).
*   **Function:** This module will encode raw item content (images or text) and map it to a sequence of discrete codes from a learnable codebook.
*   **Unified Dictionary:** The codebooks from different modalities will be merged into a single vocabulary. This allows the system to represent any item as a sequence of "words" (tokens) in this new quantitative language, regardless of its original domain or modality.
*   **Collision Handling:** To ensure every item has a unique representation, we will implement a logic that reallocates tokens for "colliding" items based on the distance between their residual vectors and the codebook vectors, ensuring unique identifiability while maintaining semantic clustering.

**2. Quantitative Language Generation Tasks (The Syntax)**
To endow these tokens with semantic meaning and prior knowledge, we will design a set of generative tasks that function like natural language processing tasks:
*   **Next Item Generation:** A standard sequence-to-sequence task predicting the token sequence of the target item based on user history.
*   **Asymmetric Item Generation:** A cross-modal task where the model uses interaction history from one modality (e.g., text tokens) to predict the target item in the other modality (e.g., image tokens). This forces the model to learn the latent correlations between visual and textual preferences.
*   **Quantitative Language Alignment:** An explicit translation task where the model learns to convert the text-based quantitative language of an item directly into its image-based quantitative language (and vice versa).

**3. Knowledge Transfer via Pre-training and Fine-tuning**
We will adopt a two-stage training paradigm:
*   **Pre-training:** The model will be pre-trained on source domain datasets using the generation tasks described above to learn the grammar and semantics of the quantitative language.
*   **Fine-tuning:** The pre-trained weights will be transferred to the target recommendation task to leverage the learned multimodal priors.
*   **Re-ranking:** During inference, we will generate candidate lists from both text and image generation sub-tasks and merge them to robustly capture user preferences.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Novelty:** We introduce the concept of a "Quantitative Language" for recommendation, shifting the paradigm from ID-prediction to a unified, multimodal language generation problem.
*   **Bridge for Transfer Learning:** The approach provides a scalable mechanism to break down barriers between different domains and modalities, facilitating efficient knowledge transfer.
*   **Scalability:** By removing reliance on traditional ID indices and utilizing a fixed-size codebook, the model offers potential scalability advantages and better generalization to unseen items (zero-shot capability).

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a comprehensive evaluation of the Multimodal Quantitative Language for Generative Recommendation (MQL4GRec) framework. The experiments were conducted to validate the method's ability to transfer recommendation knowledge across domains and modalities via a unified quantitative language.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **Source:** We utilized the Amazon Product Reviews dataset.
    *   **Pre-training Domains (Source):** Six categories were used for pre-training: "Pet Supplies", "Cell Phones and Accessories", "Automotive", "Tools and Home Improvement", "Toys and Games", and "Sports and Outdoors".
    *   **Sequential Recommendation Domains (Target):** Three categories were used for downstream evaluation: "Musical Instruments", "Arts Crafts and Sewing", and "Video Games".
    *   **Preprocessing:** We filtered out users and items with fewer than five interactions. User behavior sequences were created based on chronological order. The maximum item sequence length was set to 20.
    *   **Modality:** Each item included a title, description (text), and an image.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   We employed Top-k Recall (HR@K) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG@K).
    *   Specific K values: K = 1, 5, 10.
    *   **Evaluation Strategy:** Leave-one-out strategy. Full ranking evaluation was performed over the entire item set (not sample-based).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Non-Generative/Discriminative:** GRU4Rec, BERT4Rec, SASRec, FDSA, S^3-Rec, VQ-Rec, MISSRec.
    *   **Generative:** P5-CID (P5 with collaborative indexing), VIP5 (Multimodal P5), TIGER (Generative retrieval with semantic IDs).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Text Encoding:** We used LLaMA to encode item titles and descriptions, aggregating via mean pooling.
    *   **Image Encoding:** We used the CLIP image branch with a ViT-L/14 backbone.
    *   **Vector Quantization (RQ-VAE):** Implemented with MLPs and ReLU activation. Codebook level = 4; Codebook size per level = 256; Vector dimension = 32.
    *   **Generative Model:** We utilized the T5 framework.
        *   Structure: 4 layers for encoder and decoder.
        *   Attention: 6 self-attention heads per layer, dimension 64.
        *   MLP dimension: 1024. Input dimension: 128.
    *   **Optimization:**
        *   Optimizer: AdamW (weight decay 0.01).
        *   Pre-training: Batch size 4096, Learning rate 0.001.
        *   Fine-tuning/Alignment: Batch size 512, Max learning rate 5e-4 (cosine scheduler with warm-up).
        *   Hardware: Tesla V100 GPUs (4 for pre-training, 2 for fine-tuning).
    *   **Inference:** Beam search with a beam size of 20.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Baseline Performance:**
    *   Observation: Among non-generative methods, MISSRec generally achieved the best performance, indicating the utility of multimodal information.
    *   Observation: VIP5 (generative multimodal) did not perform well, likely due to modal differences between PLMs and image data.
    *   Observation: TIGER performed well on Instruments and Arts but lacked superiority on the Games dataset, potentially due to its lack of auxiliary content information.

*   **Collision Handling Analysis:**
    *   Observation: Including a user ID token in the input (as done in TIGER) degraded model performance, particularly on the Games dataset. This was attributed to TIGER representing tens of thousands of users with only 2000 tokens, causing high collision rates.
    *   Observation: The proposed collision handling method based on residual vector distance proved more effective than TIGER's method of adding item index layers.

*   **Impact of Pre-training Dataset Size:**
    *   Observation: For text-only quantitative language, downstream task performance gradually improved as the number of pre-training datasets increased.
    *   Observation: For multimodal quantitative language, performance improved on Instruments and Arts with more pre-training data but gradually declined on the Games dataset. This decline suggests potential overfitting or significant domain differences for the Games dataset.

*   **Impact of Pre-training Epochs:**
    *   Observation: With text-only quantitative language, downstream performance improved with more pre-training epochs, stabilizing around 25 epochs.
    *   Observation: With multimodal quantitative language, Instruments and Arts datasets reached peak performance early in the training process. Conversely, performance on the Games dataset deteriorated as pre-training epochs increased, suggesting a conflict between recommendation knowledge from different modalities or source domains.

*   **Zero-shot Analysis:**
    *   Observation: Pre-trained models demonstrated preliminary (though weak) zero-shot capabilities on Instruments and Arts datasets.
    *   Observation: Zero-shot capability was not evident on the Games dataset, likely due to data scarcity and limited model parameter size hindering generalization.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

## Optional Statements
These should appear at the end of the main text, before references.
1.  **Ethics Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Address potential concerns (human subjects, sensitive data, bias, etc.).
2.  **Reproducibility Statement:** (Optional, max 1 page) Reference code, proofs, or data processing steps to ensure reproducibility.

## Important Rules
* **Formatting:** Do not modify the width or length of the text rectangle or font sizes.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The dominant paradigm in recommendation systems (RS), IDRec, represents users and items via unique, static identifiers. While effective, this approach suffers from inherent cold-start problems and poor transferability across domains due to the non-shared nature of IDs. Recently, Generative Recommendation has emerged, leveraging Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) to predict target identifiers directly. However, significant gaps remain:
1.  **Linguistic Discrepancy:** There is a fundamental mismatch between the general linguistic knowledge embedded in PLMs and the specific, discrete needs of recommendation identifiers.
2.  **Modal Silos:** Existing methods rarely exploit the complementary knowledge between multimodal information (text and images) effectively. They typically use encoders merely for feature extraction rather than creating a unified generative space.
3.  **Inefficient Transfer:** The lack of a shared vocabulary across different domains and modalities hinders the effective transfer of recommendation knowledge.

We aim to address the inability of current systems to unify multimodal item content into a concise, transferable language that PLMs can generate natively.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **MQL4GRec (Multimodal Quantitative Language for Generative Recommendation)**. Our core hypothesis is that we can transform complex item content from diverse domains and modalities (text and image) into a unified, discrete "Quantitative Language."

By training specialized "Quantitative Translators" based on Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoders (RQ-VAE), we can map high-dimensional modal features into sequences of discrete tokens drawn from a shared vocabulary. This will allow us to treat recommendation as a sequence-to-sequence generation task where the model learns to "speak" the language of items, facilitating seamless knowledge transfer and explicit alignment between textual and visual user preferences.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Quantitative Language Construction
To bridge the gap between modalities, we will implement **Quantitative Translators** that convert item content into discrete token sequences. We will train distinct translators for text and images, which will share a unified dictionary structure.

**The Quantitative Translator (RQ-VAE):**
We will employ a frozen modal encoder to obtain the initial high-dimensional representation $h$ of an item. For text, we will use **LLaMA**; for images, we will use a **Vision Transformer (ViT)**.
This representation $h$ serves as input to a **Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (RQ-VAE)**. The RQ-VAE creates a tuple of codewords (item tokens) by recursively quantizing residuals.

Let $\mathcal{C}^l = \{ \boldsymbol{v}_k^l \}_{k=1}^K$ be the codebook at level $l$, where $K$ is the codebook size. For an input vector $\boldsymbol{z}$ (derived from $h$), the quantization process at level $i$ is defined as:

$$ c_i = \underset{k}{\arg \min} \left\| \boldsymbol{r}_i - \boldsymbol{v}_k^i \right\|_2^2 $$
$$ \boldsymbol{r}_{i+1} = \boldsymbol{r}_i - \boldsymbol{v}_{c_i}^i $$

where $\boldsymbol{r}_1 = \boldsymbol{z}$ and $\boldsymbol{r}_i$ is the residual vector at the $i$-th level. The quantized representation $\hat{z}$ is the summation of the selected code vectors across $L$ levels:
$$ \hat{z} = \sum_{i=1}^{L} \boldsymbol{v}_{c_i}^i $$

The network will be trained using a compound loss function minimizing reconstruction error and the distance between residuals and code vectors:
$$ \mathcal{L}(h) = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}} + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rqvae}} $$
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}} = \| h - \hat{h} \|_2^2 $$
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rqvae}} = \sum_{i=1}^{L} \left\| \mathrm{sg}[\boldsymbol{r}_i] - \boldsymbol{v}_{c_i}^i \right\|_2^2 + \beta \left\| \boldsymbol{r}_i - \mathrm{sg}[\boldsymbol{v}_{c_i}^i] \right\|_2^2 $$
where $\hat{h}$ is the decoder output, $\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]$ is the stop-gradient operator, and $\beta$ is the commitment cost.

**Dictionary Unification:**
To distinguish modalities within the shared vocabulary, we will apply prefixes to the generated codewords:
*   **Text Codes:** Lowercase prefixes (e.g., $V_t = \{ a\_1, b\_2, \dots, d\_K \}$).
*   **Image Codes:** Uppercase prefixes (e.g., $V_v = \{ A\_1, B\_2, \dots, D\_K \}$).
This results in a total vocabulary size of $2LK$, capable of representing $K^L$ unique items per modality.

### 2. Collision Resolution Strategy
Since multiple items might map to the same token sequence, we will implement a deterministic reallocation strategy to resolve collisions based on residual distance.
For $N$ colliding items, we calculate the distance matrix $\boldsymbol{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times L \times K}$ between residual vectors and code vectors:
$$ d_k^i = \| \boldsymbol{r}_i - \boldsymbol{v}_k^i \|_2^2 $$
We will sort items based on their minimum distance to the code vectors of the last level ($L$). We then reallocate tokens by assigning the nearest available token in the last level. If the last level is exhausted, we backtrack to the second-last level, ensuring unique identifiers for all items.

### 3. Quantitative Language Generation (QLG) Tasks
We will design specific generation tasks to imbue the quantitative language with semantic meaning and enable cross-modal transfer. The backbone model will be a **T5-based Transformer**.

**Task A: Next Item Generation (NIG)**
The primary recommendation task.
*   **Input:** Sequence of item tokens from user interaction history.
*   **Output:** Target item tokens corresponding to the respective modality (Text $\to$ Text, Image $\to$ Image).

**Task B: Asymmetric Item Generation (AIG)**
To enforce cross-modal knowledge transfer.
*   **Input:** Image tokens of interaction history.
*   **Output:** Text tokens of the target item (and vice versa).

**Task C: Quantitative Language Alignment (QLA)**
Explicit alignment to ground the modalities.
*   **Input:** Text tokens of an item.
*   **Output:** Image tokens of the *same* item (and vice versa).

### 4. Optimization and Inference
We will utilize a two-stage training paradigm:
1.  **Pre-training:** On source domain datasets using NIG tasks to learn general sequential patterns.
2.  **Fine-tuning:** On target domain datasets using all QLG tasks (NIG, AIG, QLA).

The model is optimized via negative log-likelihood:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\theta} = - \sum_{j=1}^{|\mathbf{Y}|} \log P_{\theta} (\mathbf{Y}_j \mid \mathbf{Y}_{<j}, \mathbf{X}) $$

**Inference (Re-ranking):**
We will generate two distinct recommendation lists, $R_t$ (from text sub-tasks) and $R_v$ (from image sub-tasks). We will fuse these scores to prioritize items appearing in both lists. The final score $s(x)$ for item $x$ is defined as:
$$ s(x) = \begin{cases} (s_t(x) + s_v(x)) / 2 + 1 & x \in R_t, x \in R_v \\ s_t(x) & x \in R_t \\ s_v(x) & x \in R_v \end{cases} $$

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Unified Quantitative Semantics:** We expect to establish a methodology that breaks down barriers between domains and modalities by translating them into a shared, discrete language, eliminating the need for arbitrary ID assignment.
2.  **Enhanced Knowledge Transfer:** By formalizing recommendation as a language generation task over this shared vocabulary, we anticipate significantly improved transferability of user preference patterns from source to target domains.
3.  **Cross-Modal Synergy:** The proposed asymmetric and alignment tasks should allow the model to leverage visual information to improve textual recommendations (and vice versa), capturing multi-faceted user preferences more effectively than unimodal baselines.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.name: none
agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
